unit.name: The Roman City & Home
unit.subtitle: How a Roman city was planned and built, the forum and public buildings, the town house and the apartment block, and Pompeii and Herculaneum as our evidence.

lessons.title: Town Planning & the City
lessons.description: How Roman cities were planned — the grid, the forum, and life in Rome, Ostia and Pompeii.
lessons.content_html:
Why Did Rome Build Cities?

When Rome conquered new territory, it did not simply station soldiers and move on. It built cities. Across the empire, from Britain to Syria, Roman towns followed recognisable patterns: wide streets laid out on a grid, a central forum for business and politics, public baths, temples, markets and amphitheatres. This consistency was not an accident. The Romans understood that a well-planned city reinforced Roman identity, encouraged commerce, and projected the power of the empire onto a conquered landscape. Understanding the design of a Roman city is therefore not just about architecture — it is about understanding how Rome controlled and civilised its world.

The Grid Plan

Most Roman towns were laid out on a grid plan. Two main roads formed the backbone: the cardo ran north to south and the decumanus ran east to west. They crossed at the heart of the town, usually at or near the forum. Secondary streets branched off these two main arteries, dividing the town into rectangular blocks called insulae (islands). This plan made it easy to navigate, to administer, and to expand a city in an orderly way.

Pavements lined the main streets, raised above the road surface so that pedestrians were protected from wheeled traffic and from the mud and waste that accumulated in the roadway. In Pompeii, wide stepping stones allowed people to cross from one pavement to another without descending to road level. The gaps between the stepping stones were spaced to allow cart wheels to pass through. This detail, preserved at Pompeii, tells us a great deal about the volume and type of traffic on Roman streets and the practical solutions Romans devised to manage it.

Key Fact

The Roman town grid was organised around the cardo (north–south) and the decumanus (east–west). They crossed near the forum, the civic and commercial heart of the city. This grid plan was used across the empire, from Pompeii in Italy to Timgad in North Africa.

Water Supply and Sanitation

No Roman city functioned without water. Aqueducts brought fresh water into the city from springs sometimes many kilometres away. At Pompeii, the main aqueduct fed a high-pressure water tower called a castellum aquae, from which lead and terracotta pipes distributed water to public fountains, the baths, and wealthy private houses. Most ordinary residents collected their water from the public fountains placed at regular intervals along the streets; fresh water was never more than a short walk away. Inscriptions on the water tower at Pompeii suggest that the system was carefully maintained and that officials were responsible for its upkeep.

Drainage was equally important. Deep stone-lined sewers ran beneath the streets, carrying waste water away from fountains, baths and latrines. The great Cloaca Maxima (Great Sewer) at Rome was an engineering marvel that drained the low-lying area of the Forum Romanum and discharged into the Tiber. Its construction was attributed in ancient tradition to the early kings of Rome, and it continued to function throughout the imperial period.

The Forum

The forum was the beating heart of any Roman city. At Pompeii, the main forum took the form of a large rectangular open space, measuring roughly 38 by 157 metres, surrounded on three sides by a two-storey colonnade. This colonnaded walkway provided shade for the merchants, lawyers and citizens who gathered there daily. At the north end of the forum stood the Temple of Jupiter, the most important religious building in the city, its raised podium dominating the space. On the other sides stood civic buildings: the basilica (a large covered hall for legal and commercial business), the comitium (an assembly room), and offices for the elected magistrates who governed the town.

The forum was not merely practical. It was a statement of Roman values. By placing the temple of the chief god at its head, surrounded by the buildings of law and government, the Romans visually demonstrated that their civic life was underpinned by divine authority. Statues of emperors and local benefactors stood throughout the space, reminding every visitor of the hierarchy of power that made their ordered city possible.

Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, preserving streets, buildings and even food in extraordinary detail. This makes them our richest sources for everyday Roman town life. Pompeii was a medium-sized town of perhaps 12,000 people; Herculaneum was smaller but its wealthier character is clear from the quality of its surviving houses and wall paintings. Both towns demonstrate the grid plan, the forum complex, and the full range of amenities — baths, theatres, food stalls, temples and private homes — that characterised a typical Roman city.

Ostia, the port of Rome, offers a different perspective. Because Ostia continued to be occupied and altered after the eruption that preserved Pompeii, it shows how a Roman city evolved over time. At Ostia the famous Insula of Diana — a multi-storey apartment block — illustrates how the city housed its growing population by building upwards. Taken together, Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia provide complementary evidence for Roman urban life at different social levels and different stages of development.

Streets, Shops and the Busy City

Roman streets were not quiet. The poet Juvenal, writing in the late first or early second century AD, painted a vivid picture of the dangers of navigating Rome at night: carts rumbling past, buckets of waste thrown from upper-storey windows, and the constant roar of the city. His Satire 3 describes a man who cannot sleep for the noise and who walks in fear of collapsing buildings. While Juvenal exaggerated for satirical effect, his complaints reflect genuine conditions. In Rome, wheeled traffic was banned from the city centre during daylight hours to ease congestion, so deliveries were made at night, adding to the noise.

The ground floors of buildings lining Roman streets were typically given over to shops and workshops. At Pompeii, hundreds of small commercial premises — identifiable by their wide doorways designed to allow goods and customers easy access — opened directly onto the street. Many were thermopolia: food and drink stalls with stone counters set with large ceramic jars, from which vendors served warm food to customers who had no cooking facilities at home. The inscriptions and painted notices preserved on Pompeii’s walls also reveal an active culture of political campaigning, advertising and personal messages, bringing the city to life in a way no other Roman site can match.

Key Fact

Roman towns were full of commercial activity. The thermopolia (hot food stalls) at Pompeii show that many residents ate street food rather than cooking at home. Around 80 thermopolia have been identified in Pompeii alone, suggesting that not having a kitchen was normal for ordinary city dwellers.

It is easy to think of “Roman city life” as meaning only the city of Rome itself. But the Roman empire was covered in cities, many of them following similar plans and containing similar buildings. Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia are all Italian towns, not Rome itself. This matters because they give us evidence for what life was like in a typical medium-sized Roman city, rather than in the extraordinary capital. When you use Pompeii as evidence, you should note that it was a prosperous but unremarkable town — not an imperial showpiece — and that this actually makes it more useful as evidence for ordinary Roman life.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The command word Describe asks you to say what is there — give accurate details about appearance, layout or features. For a source question on town planning (for example, a view of the Pompeii forum or a street with stepping stones), pick out specific details from the source and connect them to your knowledge. A common mistake is to write generally about “Roman cities” without anchoring your answer to the named site (Pompeii, Ostia, Herculaneum or Rome) that the question is asking about. Always name your site and say what the specific evidence reveals.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Roman cities were laid out on a grid plan centred on the cardo and decumanus, which crossed at the forum — the civic, commercial and religious heart of the city.
  • Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia give us different but complementary evidence: Pompeii’s eruption-preserved streets reveal everyday commercial life; Ostia’s apartment blocks show how cities housed their growing populations.
  • Roman city streets were busy and noisy; Juvenal’s Satire 3 describes their dangers with satirical exaggeration, while Pompeii’s stepping stones and thermopolia provide physical evidence of how Romans navigated and fed themselves in the city.

practice_questions.text: Name one of the two main roads in a Roman town grid plan.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: cardo OR decumanus (either name accepted).

practice_questions.text: Describe what the forum of Pompeii looked like and how it was used.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for up to three accurate details: e.g. large open rectangular space / surrounded by a two-storey colonnade / Temple of Jupiter at the north end / basilica and magistrates' offices on the sides / statues of emperors and benefactors / centre for civic, commercial and religious life. No marks for vague generalities; each point needs a specific feature.

practice_questions.text: Read the following passage, which paraphrases Juvenal's Satire 3. In it, a man describes the miseries of living in Rome: the constant rumble of carts at night, the fear of falling masonry from badly built upper storeys, and buckets of waste hurled from windows above. What does this source tell us about life in a Roman city? What are its limitations as evidence?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the source (carts at night, falling masonry, waste from windows) and connects each to knowledge of Roman city conditions (ban on daytime wheeled traffic, poorly built insulae, lack of sanitation). Evaluates the source's limitations with precision — Juvenal is a satirist writing for a wealthy audience; he exaggerates for comic effect and represents only one viewpoint. Reaches a supported judgement about how useful the source is.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the source and links them to knowledge. Identifies at least one limitation (satire / exaggeration / limited viewpoint) with some explanation.
Developing: Picks out a detail or two and makes a general comment about limitations without full development.
Emerging: Paraphrases the source or makes very general points about Roman city life without engaging with the text.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the grid plan was a useful design for Roman cities.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a reason; 1 mark for explaining it. Up to two explained reasons for full marks. E.g.: Easy navigation (1) — a regular street pattern meant both residents and newcomers could find their way without getting lost, making trade and administration more efficient (1). Ease of expansion (1) — new blocks could simply be added to the existing grid, allowing the city to grow in an orderly way (1). Easy administration (1) — the regular layout made it simple to identify properties, collect taxes and maintain public buildings (1). Any two well-explained reasons score full marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful are Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence for everyday life in Roman cities? Use sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues with precision, using named sources (thermopolia, stepping stones, forum colonnade, inscriptions, Insula of Diana at Ostia for comparison). Evaluates both the value of the evidence (exceptional preservation, wide range of building types, commercial and domestic detail) and its limits (both are frozen in AD 79; both are Italian towns, not the capital; Pompeii may not represent the poorest Romans). Reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Uses two or more named examples from Pompeii or Herculaneum and makes a clear argument about usefulness, with at least one evaluative point.
Developing: Describes what Pompeii reveals but does not evaluate; argument is one-sided or unsupported.
Emerging: General statements about Pompeii without named evidence.

practice_questions.text: How far do the physical remains of Pompeii give us a complete picture of Roman city life? In your answer, refer to both the evidence and its limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument using a range of named sources (e.g. thermopolia, forum layout, stepping stones, wall-paintings, graffiti inscriptions, water tower/castellum aquae). Considers both strength of evidence (extraordinary preservation; wide range of building types; evidence from both wealthy and ordinary households) and limitations (single moment in time — AD 79; not the capital; limited evidence for the very poorest; bias towards surviving stone buildings). Reaches a supported judgement about how complete the picture is, perhaps noting that Ostia or literary sources like Juvenal fill some of the gaps.
Secure: Clear argument using several named examples; evaluates both strength and limitation; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes the evidence but does not evaluate it critically; argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging: General descriptive points about Pompeii without use of specific named evidence.

lessons.title: The Forum & Public Buildings
lessons.description: The heart of Roman civic life — the forum, basilica, temples and public buildings of the Roman city.
lessons.content_html:
The Forum: Where Roman Life Happened

If you wanted to understand what Roman civic life meant, you would start at the forum. Every Roman city of any significance had one. The forum was at once a marketplace, a law court, a political meeting place, and a religious precinct. It was where magistrates announced decisions, where merchants haggled over prices, where orators addressed crowds, and where temples dominated the skyline. To enter the forum was to be reminded of everything that made a city Roman — order, law, commerce, and the goodwill of the gods. The forum of Pompeii is one of the best-preserved examples, and it repays close study as evidence for how these spaces were designed and used.

The Layout of the Forum at Pompeii

The forum at Pompeii was a large rectangular open space, roughly 38 metres wide and 157 metres long, oriented north to south. It was paved with limestone and surrounded on three sides — east, west and south — by a double-storey colonnade. This colonnade served a practical purpose: it gave shade in the Mediterranean heat and provided a sheltered space for business and conversation. At the north end rose the Temple of Jupiter on a high podium, its columns and steps visible from the length of the forum, emphasising both the importance of the chief Roman god and the god’s oversight of civic life.

Around the other sides of the forum stood a series of civic buildings. The basilica, located at the south-west corner, was the largest building in Pompeii. It measured roughly 24 by 55 metres and consisted of a tall central nave flanked by lower side aisles, separated by rows of brick columns. A raised platform at one end provided a dais from which judges could preside over legal proceedings. The basilica was not only a court but also a venue for commercial negotiations: major contracts were drawn up and witnessed under its roof. The building type would later be adopted by early Christians as a model for their churches, giving the basilica an extraordinary afterlife that the original Roman designers could not have imagined.

Key Fact

Around the Pompeii forum stood: the Temple of Jupiter (religious worship, north end), the basilica (law court and business, south-west), the comitium (voting and assembly), and the offices of magistrates. Each building served a distinct civic function, showing that the forum was the hub of all public life.

Temples in the City

Temples were not confined to the forum. They were scattered throughout Roman cities, dedicated to a wide variety of gods. In Pompeii, the Temple of Apollo stood on the western boundary of the forum precinct, enclosed within a colonnaded portico of 48 Doric columns surrounding the temple on its podium. Apollo was associated with music, prophecy, light and healing, and his temple at Pompeii was one of the oldest in the city; the building was already several centuries old by the time of the eruption in AD 79. A bronze statue of Apollo — found in the precinct and now in Naples — showed the god in the archer pose (Apollo Saettante), his arm extended forward as if releasing an arrow. The statue’s high quality indicates the wealth and civic pride that Pompeians invested in their gods.

Elsewhere in Pompeii, the Temple of Isis stood near the large theatre in the south-east of the city. This was dedicated to the Egyptian goddess Isis, whose cult spread through the Roman world from the first century BC onwards. The presence of an Isis temple in a medium-sized Italian town demonstrates how Roman cities absorbed religions from across the empire, and how the religious landscape of a Roman city was far more diverse than a simple list of the traditional Roman gods would suggest. The Isis temple was rebuilt after the earthquake of AD 62 and was decorated with vivid wall paintings depicting the myths of Isis and Osiris.

One of the most valuable types of evidence from Pompeii is its inscriptions. Hundreds of painted notices — called programmata — survive on the walls of the city, many of them near the forum. These include electoral notices endorsing candidates for the positions of aedile (who maintained public buildings and ran markets) and duumvir (the two chief magistrates of the town). One inscription preserved by Cooley and Cooley in their Pompeii: A Sourcebook reads: “The fruit sellers, together with Helvius Vestalis, urge you to elect Marcus Holconius Priscus as duumvir for the administration of justice.” This shows the involvement of tradespeople in civic politics and the competitive nature of local elections. The forum’s public face was covered in political advertising, turning the walls themselves into a kind of ancient noticeboard.

Markets and Commerce

The forum was not the only commercial space in a Roman city. Dedicated market buildings called macella provided a sheltered environment for buying and selling food and goods. In Pompeii, the macellum stood at the north-east corner of the forum. It consisted of an open courtyard with a central tholos — a small circular structure with a tiled roof supported on columns, possibly used for selling fish — surrounded by shops. Remains of fish scales and animal bones found here confirm its function. The macellum separated the messier business of food retail from the more formal civic activities at the centre of the forum.

Beyond the forum, the streets of Pompeii were lined with the premises of bakers, fullers (cloth cleaners), smiths, wine sellers and many other trades. The largest bakery discovered at Pompeii contained four stone mills (turned by donkeys or slaves), a wood-fired oven, and carbonised loaves of bread still on the shelves when the eruption came. These physical remains make it possible to reconstruct the working day of a Roman baker in extraordinary detail, and remind us that behind the grand civic architecture of the forum lay a city full of ordinary commercial and industrial activity.

Key Fact

The macellum (covered food market) at Pompeii was located immediately beside the forum, at the north-east corner. Its central tholos structure and surrounding shops show that even food trading in a Roman city was organised and architecturally formalised, not simply done from carts in the street.

The forum was not designed to be merely functional. Its buildings, statues and inscriptions worked together to communicate Roman civic ideology. The Temple of Jupiter at the head of the forum placed the chief god in symbolic authority over all the commerce, law and politics that took place beneath him. Statues of emperors and local benefactors reminded citizens of the hierarchy of power and the expectation of public generosity. When a wealthy citizen funded the restoration of a public building, an inscription recording the donation was prominently displayed, cementing both the donor’s reputation and the idea that civic prosperity was the responsibility of the wealthy. The inscription on the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche at Pompeii, for example, records how a freedwoman funded the construction of a tomb and paid for public games, demonstrating that even those of modest legal status could gain honour through public benefaction. The forum was therefore a space where Roman values of order, piety, generosity and ambition were displayed, competed over, and reinforced.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a source question shows you a building from the forum area, the command word Analyse means you should go beyond describing what you see and explain what specific features reveal about Roman values or practices. For example, if shown the basilica, do not just say “it was used as a law court” — explain why placing the law court at the forum tells us about Roman attitudes to civic order and public life. Always anchor your analysis to details in the source, not just to background knowledge.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The forum was the civic heart of a Roman city, combining religion (Temple of Jupiter), law (basilica), commerce (macellum), and politics (magistrates’ offices) in a single planned space.
  • Inscriptions on Pompeii’s walls — programmata — show that local elections were competitive and that tradespeople actively participated in civic politics.
  • The physical layout of the forum communicated Roman values: placing the chief god’s temple in the position of honour made visible the Roman belief that good governance depended on divine support.

practice_questions.text: The following is a paraphrase of a Pompeian wall inscription (programmata): 'The fruit sellers, together with Helvius Vestalis, urge you to elect Marcus Holconius Priscus as duumvir for the administration of justice.' What does this inscription reveal about civic life in Pompeii? What are its limitations as evidence?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the inscription (fruit sellers as endorsers, the named candidate, the role of duumvir for justice) and links each to knowledge of Pompeian civic life — elections were competitive; tradespeople participated in politics; duumviri were the chief magistrates. Evaluates limitations clearly: inscription only represents those who could afford public notices; we do not know whether the candidate won; survivorship of inscriptions is random. Reaches a supported judgement about usefulness.
Secure: Uses at least two details and links them to civic life; identifies one limitation with explanation.
Developing: Makes general points about elections without engaging with specific details in the inscription.
Emerging: Paraphrases the inscription without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Temple of Jupiter was placed at the north end of the forum at Pompeii.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a reason; 1 mark for explaining it. E.g.: Position of honour (1) — placing the most important god at the head of the forum, dominating the space, showed that Roman civic life was under divine authority and that Jupiter’s approval was essential for the city’s success (1). Visibility (1) — the raised podium and elevated columns meant the temple could be seen the length of the forum, reminding all who entered of the god’s importance (1). Up to two explained reasons for full marks.

practice_questions.text: How do the public buildings of Pompeii reflect Roman civic values? Use named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues clearly using named examples (basilica, Temple of Jupiter, macellum, programmata, statues of benefactors, Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche inscription). Connects each to a Roman civic value: law and order (basilica), piety (Temple of Jupiter), organised commerce (macellum), civic participation (programmata), public generosity (benefactor statues/inscriptions). Makes a clear overall argument about what these buildings collectively tell us.
Secure: Uses two or more named examples and connects each to a civic value, with clear explanation.
Developing: Describes what the buildings looked like but does not develop the link to civic values.
Emerging: General statements about the forum without named sources.

practice_questions.text: How far do the public buildings of Pompeii show us that religion was central to Roman civic life?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument using a range of named sources. For religion's importance: Temple of Jupiter at the head of the forum; Temple of Apollo in its own precinct; Temple of Isis showing diversity of worship; religious imagery in civic buildings. Counter-argument: buildings also show commerce (macellum), law (basilica), and politics (programmata, magistrates’ offices) were equally central. Reaches a supported judgement, perhaps arguing that religion was inseparable from civic life rather than separate from it.
Secure: Uses several named examples, addresses both sides, reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes religious buildings without evaluating their relative importance; one-sided argument.
Emerging: General descriptions without specific named sources.

lessons.title: The Roman Domus
lessons.description: Inside a wealthy Roman town house — the atrium, the peristyle and the rooms that displayed status.
lessons.content_html:
The Domus: A Home Designed to Impress

In a Roman city, where you lived told the world everything about who you were. The wealthy Roman town house — the domus — was not simply a private retreat. It was an arena of social performance. Its rooms were arranged to guide visitors on a carefully choreographed journey from the public street to the innermost spaces of family life, with each zone communicating a message about the owner’s wealth, taste and status. The House of Menander and the House of Octavius Quartio at Pompeii are two of the best-preserved examples, and they allow us to read that social performance in remarkable detail.

Entering the Domus: The Fauces and Atrium

A visitor approaching a wealthy domus from the street would pass through a narrow entrance corridor called the fauces (meaning throat). This passage was often decorated with mosaics warning visitors — sometimes with an image of a chained dog and the words cave canem (beware of the dog) — that not everyone was welcome. Beyond the fauces opened the atrium, the most public room of the house. The atrium had a rectangular opening in the roof called the compluvium, which let in light and air. Directly below this was the impluvium, a shallow pool that collected rainwater. The impluvium was sometimes lined with mosaic and often decorated with a small fountain.

The atrium served as both reception hall and waiting room. The patron of the household received clients here each morning during the salutatio, the formal morning greeting, when those who owed political or financial loyalty to the householder came to pay their respects. Visitors waiting in the atrium were deliberately kept in view of the household’s wealth: bronze furniture, fine floor mosaics, and family portraits (called imagines) would all be on display. The whole arrangement was designed to make an impression before a word was spoken.

Key Fact

The atrium was the main public room of a Roman domus. It had a central roof opening (the compluvium) that let in light, and a pool beneath (the impluvium) to catch rainwater. This arrangement also served as a visual centrepiece for impressing clients during the morning salutatio.

The Tablinum and the Triclinium

Behind the atrium, directly aligned with the entrance, stood the tablinum. This was the office of the householder, where the paterfamilias conducted business, received important clients, and stored household records. Its position, opening onto both the atrium and the garden beyond, allowed the owner to be visible to visitors while remaining in a position of authority. The tablinum was often richly decorated with wall paintings to emphasise the owner’s sophistication and wealth.

The grandest room for social entertainment was the triclinium. Guests reclined on three couches — giving the room its name from the Greek for “three couches” — arranged in a U-shape around low tables. At the top of the arrangement lay the most honoured position, the lectus medius summus, where the host would place his most important guest. The triclinium was decorated to maximise its visual effect: the House of Menander at Pompeii preserves a triclinium with black wall paintings framed in red and yellow borders, of a high quality that demonstrates the household’s wealth and cultural sophistication.

The Peristyle Garden

Beyond the tablinum, the house opened onto the peristyle, a colonnaded garden at the rear of the house. The peristyle was the private heart of the household, used by family rather than clients. It typically contained flower beds, statues, a fountain, and sometimes a fishpond. The colonnades provided shaded walkways and framed the garden into a formal composition. In the House of Octavius Quartio at Pompeii, the garden was exceptionally elaborate: it contained a long ornamental water channel, wall paintings of hunting scenes and mythological subjects, and a garden dining area. The paintings from this house vividly illustrate how wealthy Pompeians decorated their outdoor spaces with mythological imagery as a display of cultural knowledge and artistic patronage.

The orientation of the domus was not accidental. The arrangement from street to atrium to tablinum to peristyle created a single visual axis: a visitor standing at the door could look all the way through to the garden. This axial design was deliberately theatrical, drawing the eye through the house and giving every section its moment in the viewer’s line of sight. Even in a private home, the Romans thought architecturally about movement, sight lines and the performance of status.

Roman wall paintings in Pompeii have survived in extraordinary condition because they were protected by the volcanic ash that buried the city. Art historians have identified four main styles of Pompeian wall painting. The Second Style (roughly 80–15 BC) used painted architectural illusions to make walls appear to open onto colonnades, columns and landscapes — a trompe l’oeil effect that made rooms seem larger than they were. The Third and Fourth Styles favoured smaller mythological scenes set within elaborate architectural frames. These paintings communicated the owner’s education and cultural awareness: mythological subjects required the viewer to recognise the stories of the gods and heroes, and identifying them correctly was a sign of cultivated learning.

Floor mosaics were equally important as status symbols. The famous Cave Canem mosaic from the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet at Pompeii shows a chained dog with the Latin warning below. Its placing at the entrance was a witty display of wealth and sophistication: the mosaic demonstrates that the household could afford fine floor decoration while simultaneously keeping unwanted visitors away with a gentle joke. Mosaics throughout the house served not just as floor covering but as miniature works of art, with the finest examples — like the celebrated Alexander mosaic found at the House of the Faun at Pompeii — requiring extraordinary skill and expense to produce.

Key Fact

The layout of the domus moved from public to private: fauces (entrance passage) → atrium (public reception hall) → tablinum (owner’s office) → triclinium (dining room) → peristyle (private garden). Each zone was decorated and furnished according to how many visitors were expected to see it.

Many students assume that the domus was primarily a private, domestic space. In fact, a wealthy Roman domus was intensely public in character. The morning salutatio brought dozens of clients into the atrium; business was conducted in the tablinum; the triclinium hosted dinner parties that were social and political events as much as meals. The house was the primary arena through which a Roman aristocrat exercised patronage, built political alliances, and displayed his wealth and culture. The boundary between public and private that modern people assume was much less fixed in the Roman world. This is why the decoration of every room — even the entrance passage — was so carefully considered: every space was potentially on display.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to explain what a feature of the domus reveals about Roman values, make sure you move from the physical detail to the social meaning. Do not just say “the atrium had an impluvium” — explain why that mattered: it was the focal point of the most public room in the house, used to impress clients during the morning greeting. The biggest examiner complaint is answers that describe what a room looked like without saying what it tells us about Roman attitudes to status, social hierarchy, or the relationship between public and private life.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Roman domus was arranged from public to private: fauces → atrium (with compluvium and impluvium) → tablinum → triclinium → peristyle garden. Each space communicated the owner’s status to the visitors it was designed to receive.
  • Wall paintings and mosaics were not merely decoration — they were displays of wealth and cultural knowledge, with mythological scenes requiring an educated audience to appreciate them fully.
  • The domus was as much a public performance space as a home: the morning salutatio (client greeting) and the cena (dinner party) made the house an arena of social and political life.

lessons.title: Apartment Living: the Insula
lessons.description: How ordinary Romans lived — the insula apartment block, urban hazards, and life without luxury.
lessons.content_html:
The Other Side of Roman Housing

The grand atrium houses of Pompeii paint a compelling picture of Roman domestic life, but they represent only the wealthiest fraction of the urban population. The majority of Romans in any city — the merchants, craftsmen, freedmen, labourers and the poor — did not live in sprawling domus houses with colonnaded gardens. They lived in insulae (singular: insula): multi-storey blocks of rented accommodation that crowded the streets of every Roman city. Understanding the insula is essential for understanding the full reality of Roman urban life, not just its gilded highlights.

The Insula of Diana at Ostia

The best-preserved example of a Roman insula is the Insula of Diana at Ostia, the port city of Rome. This building, which survives to a height of approximately four storeys in some parts, gives us a clear picture of how a mid-range apartment block was designed and used. The Insula of Diana takes its name from a terracotta relief of the goddess Diana (the Roman goddess of hunting, equivalent to the Greek Artemis) found on one of its facades. The block was built around a central courtyard with a fountain, which provided residents with access to water. Around the courtyard on each floor ran corridors giving access to individual apartment units.

The ground floor of the Insula of Diana was given over largely to commercial premises: taverns and shops whose wide doorways opened directly onto the street. This arrangement was typical of Roman insulae throughout the empire: the most accessible and commercially valuable space — ground level with street frontage — was used for business, while living quarters occupied the upper floors. The rental value of the lower floors was high; a taberna at ground level in a busy Roman city could command a substantial income for its landlord.

Key Fact

The Insula of Diana at Ostia survives to approximately four storeys and is organised around a central courtyard with a fountain. The ground floor contained shops and taverns; the upper floors held rented apartment units. This is the standard arrangement for Roman insulae across the empire.

Life Inside an Insula Apartment

Life in an insula apartment was very different from life in a domus. Apartments on the lower floors were more spacious and better lit; those on the upper floors were cramped, darker and further from the street. Most insula apartments had no kitchen and no private latrine. Residents cooked, when they cooked at all, on small portable braziers that burned charcoal, or they bought food from the thermopolia (hot food stalls) that lined the streets below. Water had to be fetched from public fountains; there was no running water above the ground floor. Human waste was disposed of in public latrines or, less respectably, thrown from windows into the street — a practice that the satirist Juvenal described with biting scorn in his Satire 3.

Noise and smell were constant companions in insula living. Workshops, taverns and market stalls occupied the street level; carts delivering goods to the city rumbled past at night; neighbours were never far away. Privacy, in any modern sense, barely existed. And yet the insula was not simply a slum. The better apartments at Ostia and elsewhere were equipped with mosaic floors and wall paintings of a modest quality, suggesting that their occupants had some disposable income and took pride in their surroundings. The social range of insula residents was wide, from the modestly comfortable freedman who rented a lower-floor apartment to the genuinely poor family crowded into a single room at the top of the building.

The insula posed serious dangers to its inhabitants. Fire was the greatest risk. With no running water upstairs, no kitchen facilities — forcing residents to cook on open braziers — and buildings constructed partly of timber, fires spread rapidly through the upper floors. Rome suffered catastrophic fires repeatedly throughout its history; the Emperor Nero was famously associated with a fire that destroyed much of the city in AD 64, though ancient accounts of his responsibility are not reliable. In response to the threat of fire, Roman authorities issued regulations limiting the height of insulae (Augustus reportedly set the limit at 20 metres; later emperors adjusted this), but enforcement was irregular and owners routinely violated the rules.

Structural collapse was an equally pressing danger. Landlords who built quickly and cheaply to maximise profit often skimped on foundations and materials. Juvenal mocked the flimsiness of Roman apartment buildings: he described how a single crack in the wall could presage the collapse of an entire structure, and how a wealthy Roman who could afford a house in the hills was far safer than the poor man clinging to his room at the top of a swaying insula. Pliny’s letters, written in the late first and early second century AD, also allude to the chaotic and dangerous conditions of urban life, providing a complementary literary source to Juvenal’s satirical exaggeration.

Insula versus Domus: Rich and Poor in the Same City

The contrast between the domus and the insula tells us much about how Roman society was organised. A wealthy domus owner occupied a single-storey house that spread outward over a large ground-floor footprint, with rooms arranged for the performance of status. The insula resident lived in a vertical stack of rented rooms, with no control over the building, no permanent water supply, no private outdoor space, and no ability to use the home as a stage for social performance. The two building types existed side by side in Roman cities: in Pompeii, a fine atrium house might share a block with a row of cramped rented rooms. This proximity made the social contrasts of Roman city life constantly visible.

The Roman writer Petronius, in his satirical novel the Satyricon, gives fictional but revealing portraits of freedmen who have made money and now live in the messy borderland between insula and aspiration. In the famous “Dinner with Trimalchio” episode (Satyricon 26–78), the nouveau riche freedman Trimalchio throws an extravagant dinner party that satirises Roman snobbery about wealth, taste and social status. The elaborate and excessive banquet — with course after absurd course, live entertainments, and a host who reads his own will aloud to his guests — is Petronius’s vehicle for mocking a social world where money could buy the trappings of high status but not genuine refinement.

Key Fact

The main dangers of insula living were fire (from open braziers and timber construction) and structural collapse (from cheap building). Roman authorities tried to limit insula heights, but regulations were poorly enforced. Juvenal’s Satire 3 and Pliny’s letters both describe the hazards of urban apartment life from different literary perspectives.

We have two main types of source for insula life: material remains (the Insula of Diana at Ostia) and literary descriptions (Juvenal’s Satire 3, Petronius’s Satyricon). These complement each other but each has limitations. The Insula of Diana is physical evidence — it tells us about building design, scale and materials — but it cannot tell us about the daily experience of living there, the noise, the smells, the social tensions. Literary sources give us the lived experience, but both Juvenal and Petronius were writing for educated, wealthy audiences and had satirical purposes: Juvenal exaggerated dangers for comic effect, and Petronius’s Trimalchio is a caricature. The best approach is to use both types of source together, checking each against the other, and remaining alert to the purposes and perspectives of each author.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For any question about insula life, remember to use both material evidence (the Insula of Diana at Ostia — its layout, height, courtyard fountain, ground-floor shops) and literary sources (Juvenal’s Satire 3 on fire risks and structural collapse; Petronius’s Satyricon on freedmen’s social aspirations). When evaluating a source, always comment on why the author is writing — Juvenal is a satirist; he exaggerates. That does not make him useless, but it means you must judge his claims carefully. The command word Analyse expects you to pick out specific details and explain what they reveal, not just describe what you see.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The insula (apartment block) was the most common housing type for ordinary Romans. The Insula of Diana at Ostia, surviving to approximately four storeys, is the best-preserved example, with shops on the ground floor and rented apartments above.
  • Insula life was characterised by cramped conditions, no private water supply above ground level, no kitchen, constant noise, and the serious dangers of fire and structural collapse.
  • Literary sources (Juvenal’s Satire 3, Petronius’s Satyricon) and material evidence (the Insula of Diana) complement each other but each has limitations: Juvenal exaggerates, and the Insula of Diana cannot tell us about lived experience.

But both illuminate real conditions: Juvenal’s fire and noise are corroborated by the building evidence. Reaches a supported judgement about how realistic the picture is and how the sources must be used together.

lessons.title: Pompeii & Herculaneum as Evidence
lessons.description: How Vesuvius preserved two Roman towns in AD 79, what they reveal, and the limits of the evidence.
lessons.content_html:
The Day Vesuvius Erupted

On a day in late October AD 79 (the date is now placed in October by most scholars, based on inscriptions and botanical evidence, rather than the traditional August date), the citizens of Pompeii and Herculaneum were going about their ordinary business — buying bread, mending clothes, arguing in the forum, visiting the baths — when Mount Vesuvius, the volcano looming above the Bay of Naples, erupted with catastrophic force. The eruption began in the late morning and lasted over eighteen hours. Pompeii was buried under approximately four to six metres of volcanic ash and pumice; Herculaneum, closer to the volcano, was engulfed by a series of pyroclastic surges — fast-moving rivers of superheated gas and volcanic material — that carbonised wood, boiled fluids inside sealed containers, and buried the town under up to twenty metres of hardened volcanic rock. Thousands died. The towns disappeared, unexcavated for over sixteen centuries, until the systematic excavations that began at Herculaneum in 1738 and Pompeii in 1748 began to reveal what lay beneath.

What those excavations revealed was extraordinary: two Roman towns preserved at the moment of their destruction, with streets, buildings, food, clothing, tools, furniture, wall paintings, mosaics, graffiti and human remains still in place. No other site in the ancient world offers anything like this level of detail about ordinary Roman life. Yet the very uniqueness of the evidence also raises questions about how representative these towns are — and historians have debated this for centuries.

Pliny the Younger as a Literary Source

The eruption of Vesuvius was witnessed by Pliny the Younger, who was staying at Misenum, across the bay, with his uncle Pliny the Elder (who commanded the Roman fleet and died attempting to rescue survivors). In two letters to the historian Tacitus, written some years after the event, Pliny the Younger described in vivid detail what he saw: a cloud rising from Vesuvius like a pine tree; his uncle’s decision to sail towards the disaster to help; the falling pumice stones; the darkness; the screaming crowds; and finally, the news that his uncle had died of asphyxiation on the beach at Stabiae. These two letters (Pliny, Letters 6.16 and 6.20) are among the most famous in all Latin literature, and they provide the main literary account of the eruption.

As a source, Pliny’s letters are invaluable but require careful handling. He was not in Pompeii or Herculaneum himself, so his account of conditions there is at second hand. He was also writing with a literary and self-promoting purpose: to present his uncle as a hero and to place himself as a composed observer in the face of terror. The letters were written for a literary audience and were intended to be read aloud and circulated among educated Romans. They are therefore shaped by rhetorical conventions and the desire to impress, not simply to inform.

Key Fact

Pliny the Younger wrote two famous letters to Tacitus (Letters 6.16 and 6.20) describing the AD 79 eruption. He was at Misenum across the bay, not in Pompeii itself. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, died attempting to help survivors. The letters are vivid literary accounts shaped by rhetorical purpose as well as eyewitness experience.

What Pompeii Reveals: Graffiti and Inscriptions

One of the most distinctive categories of evidence from Pompeii is its graffiti and painted wall inscriptions. Over 11,000 Latin inscriptions have been recorded from Pompeii alone. Some are electoral notices (programmata), endorsing candidates for local magistracies. Others are graffiti in the modern sense: scratched or painted personal messages recording declarations of love, insults, jokes, financial records, and even literary quotations. The collection known as Cooley and Cooley’s Pompeii: A Sourcebook catalogues many of the most important inscriptions, making them accessible to students.

Among the most revealing inscriptions are the Pompeii election notices. One set of programmata, for example, records endorsements from bakers, fruit-sellers, gold-smiths and other trade groups, demonstrating that local elections involved active participation from a wide range of the town’s commercial community. Other inscriptions include gladiatorial announcements, advertisements for properties to let, and lists of prices for goods and services. Taken together, the inscriptions turn the walls of Pompeii into a kind of community noticeboard, capturing the preoccupations and voices of its inhabitants in a way that formal historical texts cannot match.

Herculaneum was buried differently from Pompeii. The pyroclastic surges that destroyed it were so intense that they carbonised organic material rather than simply burying it. This has led to the extraordinary preservation of wooden furniture, food, textiles and even papyrus scrolls (the Villa of the Papyri yielded hundreds of carbonised scrolls, mostly philosophical texts, that scholars are still working to read using new imaging technology). The House of the Wooden Partition at Herculaneum preserves its original upper-storey wooden partition wall — a type of structural element that has not survived at Pompeii — giving us rare direct evidence of how Roman houses were constructed above ground level. The Central (Forum) Baths at Herculaneum preserve their interior fittings in better condition than the baths at Pompeii, allowing detailed study of Roman bathing architecture.

Herculaneum was a smaller and evidently wealthier town than Pompeii. Its streets are narrower, its houses more uniformly prosperous, and the absence of the commercial graffiti so abundant at Pompeii suggests a different social character. The differences between the two towns remind us that there was not one single “Roman city life” but a variety of urban experiences shaped by local character, economic activity, and social composition.

The Value and Limits of the Evidence

The evidence from Pompeii and Herculaneum is extraordinary, but historians must be alert to its limitations. Both towns are preserved at a single moment in time — AD 79 — and both were in an unusual state at the time of the eruption: Pompeii had suffered a major earthquake in AD 62 that had disrupted normal life for seventeen years, meaning that many buildings were still under repair when the volcano struck. The population that fled (or tried to flee) was not a normal cross-section of Roman society; the very poor and the very rich may have been under-represented in the physical evidence left behind. And both towns are in southern Italy, which was in some respects different from the city of Rome itself, or from cities elsewhere in the empire.

Nevertheless, the sheer quantity and variety of evidence — buildings, objects, inscriptions, human remains, food, tools — means that Pompeii and Herculaneum remain the single most important set of sources for everyday Roman urban life. No other ancient site comes close. The key is to use the evidence carefully: naming specific sites and specific finds, comparing material evidence with literary sources such as Pliny, Juvenal and Petronius, and remaining alert to what the evidence cannot tell us as well as what it can.

Key Fact

The main limitations of Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence: (1) both are frozen at AD 79, not representative of the whole span of Roman history; (2) Pompeii was disrupted by the AD 62 earthquake; (3) both are provincial Italian towns, not Rome itself; (4) the poor and transient population may be under-represented. The main strengths: unique depth of preservation; wide range of building types; ordinary commercial and domestic life captured; inscriptions and graffiti record ordinary voices.

The physical evidence of Pompeii and Herculaneum gains much of its meaning when read alongside literary sources. Pliny’s letters give us a human perspective on the eruption itself. Juvenal’s Satire 3 describes the noise, squalor and danger of city streets in terms that match what we find in the material evidence. Petronius’s Satyricon provides a fictional but vivid account of a freedman’s dinner party that illuminates the social world behind the houses we excavate. Horace’s Satires describe the pleasures and frustrations of Roman urban life from the perspective of a man of letters. None of these authors is a neutral witness: each writes with literary purposes, for a specific audience, and with his own social position. But each provides a layer of human experience that the physical remains alone cannot supply. The best historical judgements about Roman city life draw on both types of source together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to evaluate Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence, the strongest answers weigh both the strengths (unique preservation, wide range of evidence, inscriptions capturing ordinary voices) and the limitations (frozen at AD 79, disrupted by the AD 62 earthquake, provincial Italian towns not Rome itself). Avoid treating “it was preserved by the volcano” as your only strength — examiners want to see that you understand what kinds of things were preserved and why they matter. Always name specific sites or finds: the Insula of Diana, the Forum Baths at Herculaneum, Pliny’s letters, the graffiti. Vague references to “Pompeii shows us...” without a specific example will not score highly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving streets, buildings, inscriptions, graffiti, food and human remains in extraordinary detail, making them our richest source for everyday Roman urban life.
  • Pliny the Younger’s two letters to Tacitus (6.16 and 6.20) provide the main literary account of the eruption; they are vivid but shaped by rhetorical purpose and were written by someone who was not in either town.
  • The evidence has significant limits: both towns are frozen at a single moment; Pompeii was disrupted by an earthquake seventeen years earlier; both are provincial Italian towns, not Rome; and the surviving evidence may under-represent the very poorest residents.

practice_questions.text: In which year did the eruption of Vesuvius destroy Pompeii and Herculaneum?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: AD 79.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the eruption of Vesuvius affected Pompeii and Herculaneum differently.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for up to three accurate contrasts: e.g. Pompeii buried under ash and pumice (4–6 metres) / Herculaneum engulfed by pyroclastic surges / Herculaneum buried under up to 20 metres of hardened volcanic rock / Herculaneum's organic materials (wood, papyrus, food) carbonised and better preserved / Pompeii's buildings preserved but wooden elements largely gone / Herculaneum smaller and evidently wealthier / the difference in burial method explains the different types of preservation at each site.

practice_questions.text: The following paraphrases Pliny the Younger's letter to Tacitus (Letters 6.16): Pliny describes how his uncle ordered his ships to sail towards the disaster to rescue survivors, and how a vast dark cloud shaped like a pine tree rose from Vesuvius, blotting out the sun. What does this source reveal about the eruption? How reliable is it as evidence for conditions in Pompeii on that day?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the source (fleet sent to rescue; pine-tree cloud; sun blotted out) and connects each to knowledge of the eruption (eruption column rising to high altitude; scale of the disaster; Roman civic response). Evaluates reliability precisely: Pliny was at Misenum across the bay, not in Pompeii; he wrote years after the event; his letters are literary works shaped by rhetorical convention; his aim was partly to honour his uncle as a hero. This does not make the source false, but it means its perspective is partial. Reaches a supported judgement.
Secure: Uses two source details with explanation; evaluates reliability with at least one specific point about Pliny's perspective or purpose.
Developing: Describes what the source says; makes a general comment about reliability.
Emerging: Paraphrases the source without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the graffiti and inscriptions from Pompeii are a particularly valuable type of evidence for Roman city life.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a reason; 1 mark for explaining it. E.g.: Ordinary voices (1) — unlike formal literary sources which were written by educated elite men for elite audiences, graffiti records the messages, jokes and opinions of a much wider range of people, including traders, supporters of gladiators, and individuals who could not otherwise be heard in the historical record (1). Variety (1) — the inscriptions include election notices, property advertisements, prices, and personal messages, revealing the range of activities and preoccupations of daily life in a way formal sources cannot match (1). Up to two explained reasons for full marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do the material remains of Pompeii and Herculaneum provide a complete picture of Roman city life? Refer to both the strengths and limitations of the evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses named evidence for both strengths (thermopolia, graffiti, House of the Wooden Partition at Herculaneum, Forum Baths, Pliny’s letters as literary complement) and limitations (frozen at AD 79; Pompeii disrupted by AD 62 earthquake; both are provincial towns; poor may be under-represented). Argues clearly toward a judgement about how complete the picture is.
Secure: Uses two or more named examples; addresses both sides; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes the evidence without evaluating its limits; one-sided.
Emerging: General statements without specific named evidence.

practice_questions.text: How useful are literary sources such as Pliny the Younger, Juvenal and Petronius alongside the physical evidence of Pompeii and Herculaneum for understanding Roman city life?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument drawing on specific literary evidence (Pliny Letters 6.16/6.20: eruption; Juvenal Satire 3: fire, noise, street dangers; Petronius Satyricon: freedman dinner party and social aspiration; Horace Satires: pleasures of city life) alongside material evidence (Pompeii buildings, inscriptions, Herculaneum organic preservation). Evaluates each literary source: Pliny not in the town; Juvenal exaggerates for satire; Petronius is fiction. Argues that literary and physical sources complement each other because each covers gaps left by the other. Reaches a supported judgement about relative usefulness.
Secure: Uses several named literary and material sources; evaluates their limitations; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes sources without comparing or evaluating them.
Emerging: General statements about Pompeii and literature without named evidence.

glossary_terms.definition: A Roman author and lawyer (c. AD 61–113) whose letters include vivid accounts of Roman life and the AD 79 eruption of Vesuvius.
Painted public election notices on the walls of Roman buildings, endorsing candidates for local magistracies.
Scratched or painted personal messages on Roman walls, recording love declarations, insults, jokes, financial records and literary quotations.
